title: MCP Tool Registry
description: Which MCP tools agents may reach for, which composed chains are worth preferring over ad-hoc tool use, and what happens when a connector is unavailable. Held in config rather than inlined into agent files so an organization can change its MCP fleet without editing agent prose, and so no org-specific tool name leaks into a shared agent file.

defaults.description: What is on before anyone chooses anything. An empty enabledConnectors list is the deliberate default: every MCP tool description is always-on context competing with the discovery budget for the same window, so a connector should be switched on by a person who wants it, not inherited by everyone who installed the plugin.

enabledConnectors.description: Connectors enabled out of the box. The ceiling on how many may be enabled at once lives in config/token-budgets.json under mcpSurface.

toolGlobs.description: Patterns for tool names an agent is permitted to call. A glob rather than an enumeration because MCP servers add tools between releases, and a list that has to be updated before a new tool can be used is a list that will be out of date exactly when it matters.

toolChains.description: Named sequences that do a common job in a known-good order, keyed by chain name. The value of a chain is not that it is shorter — it is that it fixes the order, and the wrong order is where the cost goes: opening candidate files one at a time before searching, or editing five files before finding out the first one broke the build.

sequence.description: Tools in the order they should be called.

useWhen.description: The situation this chain is for, stated concretely enough to pick between chains without reading all of them.

budgetPerStep.description: Character budget for each step's output. A chain with no per-step ceiling spends the whole window on step one when step one happens to match a large file.

savesVersus.description: The worse approach this chain replaces. Written as the concrete alternative rather than as a saving, because the alternative is checkable and a percentage would be invented.

optional.description: Connectors that some agents want but none require, keyed by connector name. Every entry must declare a fallback: a system whose behaviour when a connector is missing is undefined does not degrade, it improvises, and improvising about a ticket number produces a ticket number that does not exist.

requiredBy.description: Agents or skills that reach for this connector, so the blast radius of it being down is readable before it is down.

fallback.description: What to do instead when the connector is unavailable — and, as importantly, what not to claim. 'Emit the specs as files; do not claim they were executed' is a fallback; 'retry' is not.

healthCheck.description: A cheap probe used to decide whether the connector is answering.

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait before treating the connector as unavailable. Short on purpose: the point of the probe is to reach the fallback quickly, and a probe that waits as long as the real call has saved nothing.

healthPolicy.description: When a connector is treated as unhealthy and what happens then.

markUnhealthyAfterFailures.description: Consecutive failures before the connector is marked down. One is defensible here: the failure being detected is usually a timeout, and paying that timeout repeatedly to gather evidence costs more than the evidence is worth.

recheckAfterSeconds.description: How long a connector stays marked down before it is probed again. Without a recheck interval, a connector that recovered stays disabled for the life of the session.

onUnhealthy.description: The policy in words. Fail fast and take the declared fallback — a carefully specified fallback that is never reached because the caller keeps retrying a timeout is decoration.

statePath.description: Where health state is recorded. Machine-scoped rather than repo-scoped, so a terminal session, a CI job and the view plane agree about which connectors are down.
